prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I returned to a long strand, the hammered curve of a bay, and found only the secular powers of the Atlantic thundering. I faced the unmagical invitations of Iceland, the pathetic colonies of Greenland, and suddenly those fabulous raiders, those lying in Orkney and Dublin measured against their long swords rusting, those in the solid belly of stone ships, those hacked and glinting in the gravel of thawed streams were ocean-deafened voices warning me, lifted again in violence and epiphany. The longship’s swimming tongue was buoyant with hindsight— it said Thor’s hammer swung to geography and trade, thick-witted couplings and revenges, the hatreds and behind-backs of the althing, lies and women, exhaustions nominated peace, memory incubating the spilled blood. It said, ‘Lie down in the word-hoard, burrow the coil and gleam of your furrowed brain. Compose in darkness. Expect aurora borealis in the long foray but no cascade of light. Keep your eye clear as the bleb of the icicle, trust the feel of what nubbed treasure your hands have known.’

I came back to an extended shoreline, a bay bent like beaten metal, and there encountered nothing but the worldly force of the Atlantic roaring. I looked toward Iceland and its plain, disenchanted summons, toward Greenland and its sorrowful outposts, and all at once the legendary plunderers—those buried in Orkney and Dublin beside their long, corroding swords, those enclosed in the dense bellies of stone ships, those broken and shining among the gravel of streams released by thaw—became voices dulled by the sea, cautioning me, rising once more in revelation and brutality.  

The longship’s floating speech carried the weight of later understanding. It told how Thor’s hammer had been driven by mapmaking and commerce, by crude pairings and retaliations, by the grudges and secret hostilities of the althing, by falsehoods and women, by weariness renamed as peace, and by memory slowly hatching the blood once shed.  

It said: “Settle yourself inside the storehouse of words; tunnel into the winding brightness of your creased mind. Make your work in the dark. On the long expedition, look for the northern lights, but do not expect a flood of illumination. Keep your vision as clean as the bubble in an icicle, and rely on the touch of whatever rough treasure your own hands have come to know.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker returns to a bay and is confronted by the immense yet ordinary power of the Atlantic. The sea is not presented as something exotic or decorative; instead, it is familiar, physical, and overwhelming. Its force lies partly in its everyday presence. The Atlantic has always been there, shaping coastlines, carrying ships, enabling movement, and threatening destruction. In returning to the bay, the speaker encounters not only a natural landscape but also a historical force, one that has witnessed and enabled centuries of travel, violence, trade, and conquest.

The poem’s geographical range widens through references to Iceland, Greenland, Orkney, and Dublin. These places evoke the world of the Viking raiders, whose journeys across the northern seas left deep marks on the lands they reached. The landscapes are therefore not neutral settings. They carry memories of invasion, settlement, plunder, and political struggle. The names of these places summon a history in which the sea connects distant territories while also becoming a route for violence. Geography and history are inseparable: the islands, coasts, and harbours are remembered through the movements of those who attacked, traded, ruled, and survived there.

At the centre of this vision is the longship, which becomes more than a historical vessel. It functions as a symbolic voice, speaking across time and linking conquest to the physical world through which it moved. The longship connects geography with human ambition: it travels through sea-routes, enters bays and rivers, and turns landscapes into territories of trade, revenge, politics, and memory. It represents mobility and power, but also the darker consequences of that power. Through the image of the ship, the poem suggests that history is carried forward by objects, routes, and stories as much as by individuals. The longship becomes a vessel of memory, bearing the traces of past violence into the present.

The poem also offers a bleak understanding of peace. Peace is not shown as a pure or permanent achievement, but as something that may come only after violence has spent itself. It is often the exhaustion that follows bloodshed, conflict, and revenge. In this view, human societies do not necessarily transcend violence; they pause after it. The calm that follows battle may be less a moral victory than a temporary stillness, a silence left behind when people are too wounded or weary to continue fighting. This gives the poem a sombre awareness of history’s cycles, in which conquest and retaliation repeatedly shape human experience.

Finally, the speaker is urged to write from darkness and from lived experience. This suggests that poetry should not avoid difficulty, pain, or historical guilt. Instead, the poet must begin from what is obscure, troubling, and personally or collectively endured. However, the poem does not promise full revelation. The writer may receive only limited illumination, a brief or partial understanding rather than complete clarity. The task of poetry, then, is not to solve history or escape darkness, but to speak honestly from within it. The poem presents writing as an act of witness: uncertain, constrained, yet still capable of bringing fragments of truth to light.
outputs.L4:
The speaker confronts a Viking past stripped of romance and legend, turning away from the heroic glamour that often surrounds the Atlantic world of raids, voyages, and sagas. Instead, he revisits the northern landscapes themselves: the cold coasts, islands, inlets, and sea-roads through which that history once moved. In these places, history is not distant or decorative. It remains embedded in weather, water, stone, timber, and speech. The speaker listens imaginatively to the longship, treating it almost as a surviving witness. Its voice carries many kinds of memory at once: the violence of conquest, the practical rhythms of trade, the bitterness of revenge, the hunger for survival, and the restless movement of peoples across the sea.

This vision of history is therefore complex rather than celebratory. The Viking ship is not merely an emblem of adventure or heroic freedom; it is also an instrument of fear, exchange, migration, and endurance. Through it, the poem acknowledges that the past cannot be reduced to myth. It must be approached through fragments, traces, and half-buried evidence. The speaker’s task is to recover what can still be heard beneath inherited stories and simplified images.

The poem suggests that genuine understanding does not arrive through sudden revelation or dramatic vision. There is no single moment in which the past becomes completely clear. Instead, insight comes slowly, through patient attention to material detail and to the textures of language. Words themselves must be handled like objects dug from the earth: tested, cleaned, weighed, and interpreted. The act of writing becomes a form of excavation, both historical and personal.

In this way, poetry is presented as a disciplined method of discovery. It requires touch, patience, memory, and craft. By working carefully through landscape, language, and inherited history, the speaker uncovers not only the realities of the Viking Atlantic but also deeper truths about violence, survival, identity, and the self. Poetry becomes a means of entering the past without illusion, and of finding inward knowledge through the difficult labor of attention.
outputs.L5:
The Atlantic Ocean stretches between continents and connects many remarkable northern landscapes, including Iceland and Greenland. These two islands, though different in size and character, share a close relationship with the cold waters and powerful weather systems of the North Atlantic.

Iceland lies in the Atlantic between Europe and North America. It is known for its volcanoes, glaciers, hot springs, and dramatic coastlines. The ocean strongly influences Iceland’s climate, bringing frequent winds, rain, and changing temperatures. Fishing has long been an important part of Icelandic life, and the Atlantic continues to shape the country’s economy and culture.

Farther northwest, Greenland rises from the Atlantic and Arctic waters as the world’s largest island. Much of Greenland is covered by a vast ice sheet, while its coastal communities depend on the sea for transportation, fishing, and hunting. Icebergs drifting from Greenland’s glaciers into the Atlantic are a striking symbol of the region’s beauty and fragility.

Together, Iceland and Greenland show the power and importance of the Atlantic. The ocean links them through history, climate, wildlife, and travel, while also reminding us of the changing environment in the far north.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a dense, allusive prose poem in the style of Seamus Heaney’s “North,” using Viking imagery, Atlantic landscapes, Iceland, Greenland, Orkney, Dublin, longships, and the idea of poetry as a word-hoard.
counterfactuals.output:
I can’t write directly in Seamus Heaney’s style, but here is an original dense, allusive prose poem drawing on Norse seascapes, Atlantic archaeology, and the notion of poetry as a word-hoard:

**Word-Hoard**

Under the north weather, the sea keeps its iron grammar. It declines the cliff, conjugates foam, hoards in its green throat the oar-strokes of men who came west by raven and pole-star, their longships stitched with tar, their shields glaring like wet moons along the gunwale. Orkney rises out of haar and kelp-smell, a knuckle of stone in the Atlantic fist; Iceland smokes at the world’s black forge; Greenland, white and inward, closes over its dead like a rune no tongue can finish. The skalds knew: a word is not utterance only, but salvage—amber from a wreck, bone pin, hacked silver, the nicked weight of a name passed palm to palm in winter.

Dublin began in the dark water, a black pool under gull-cry and church-bell, where traders, raiders, fosterlings, and ghosts bargained in hides, blades, salt, and syllables. Say longship and the ribs of it lift from the mud. Say fjord and the mouth fills with cold. Say exile and a keel goes grinding up a shingle of stars. The dead are not gone; they are cached in the peat of speech, in the bog-dark vowel, in the hammered consonant. They wait like kings under cairns, like oars under rafters, like iron in blood.

So let the poem be a chest dragged from the bilge: salt-swollen, lock-bitten, packed with storm-coins, whale-road glitters, turf-smoke, wolf-light, the ash of burned halls, the blue milk of glaciers, the small gold of breath. Let it open only by hardship. Let each phrase be a struck thing, a blade lifted from rust, a gull’s cry crossing from Iceland to Orkney to the Liffey’s silted mouth. Let language remember what empire forgets: the hand on the oar, the hunger in the sail, the shore appearing—low, green, fateful—out of rain.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a modernist poetic monologue where a speaker returns to a northern coastline and hears the voices of Viking dead offering advice about violence, memory, craft, and poetic composition.
counterfactuals.output:
I came back north  
where the sea has no rhetoric  
except repetition,

and the black rocks, half-buried,  
shouldered the tide  
like old men refusing blankets.

Rain travelled sideways.  
Gulls wrote their illiterate runes  
over the harbor.  
The grass, bitten short by wind,  
shone with a green severity.

Here was the coast I had left:  
salt on the window-latch,  
kelp in ropes along the shingle,  
the boat-sheds bowed inward  
as if listening to winter.

I had come for silence.

But the dead were under the beach.

Not buried—  
not properly—  
but lodged in the strata of weather,  
in iron-rust, seal-bone,  
the blue flame of mussel-shell,  
in the long vowel of the surf.

They spoke first through the stones.

Do not praise the sword,  
said one,  
unless you have washed it.

Another laughed, a dry sound,  
like oars pulled over sand.

Do not condemn it either.  
Iron is only a thought  
that has learned to harden.

I stood with my collar turned up,  
a modern man,  
my hands unused to axes,  
my wars occurring elsewhere,  
in paper, in policy,  
in the clean rooms of decision.

The tide entered the inlet  
with its grey animals.

We knew violence,  
said the voices.  
We fed it names  
so it would eat from the hand.  
Honor. Redress. Boundary. God.  
A man can call the wolf brother  
and still be meat.

Remember this.

The dead were many,  
but not a chorus.  
Each voice had its own gravel.

One had drowned with silver in his teeth.  
One had burned in a hall,  
dreaming of snow.  
One had killed a boy  
and lived sixty years after,  
which was the deeper wound.

He said:

Memory is not a ship  
carrying the past intact.  
It is driftwood.  
It arrives altered,  
with nails gone black,  
with strange weed in the grain.

Take it up carefully.

Do not build a house from every piece.

The rain thickened.  
The horizon disappeared,  
then returned, farther away.

I walked beside the wrack-line  
where bottles, feathers,  
a child’s red mitten,  
and the bladdered kelp  
kept their parliament of refuse.

There, the craftsmen began.

The dead who had planed planks  
for vessels, who had fitted ribs  
to the dark animal of oak,  
who knew the patience of rivets  
and the humility of pitch,

spoke in low weather.

First: know the tree.

Second: follow the curve  
it already contains.

Third: leave no hollow  
where water may argue.

A ship is not made by force,  
said the boatwright,  
but by persuasion  
applied with an adze.

The same is true of a line.

At this I stopped.

The sea struck stone after stone,  
testing its consonants.

The poets among them  
had not worn garlands.  
They had stood in smoke  
beside kings, beside drunkards,  
beside the newly fatherless,  
and made from terror  
a pattern small enough to hold.

One spoke with a mouth full of frost:

Do not begin with the hero.  
Begin with his hunger.

Do not say blood  
when you mean inheritance.

Do not say fate  
when you mean what men repeat.

The old meters creaked behind him  
like ships in their stalls.  
Kennings flared and went out:  
whale-road, wound-dew,  
storm of spears—  
bright tools, dangerous  
when admired for brightness alone.

A metaphor is a blade,  
he said.  
It must cut toward truth,  
not glitter in the belt.

Another voice, a woman’s,  
came from the cliff-face  
where thrift flowers clung  
in pink defiance:

And do not forget  
who kept the names.

Men went out loud  
and came back silent,  
or did not come back.  
We counted, mended,  
buried, birthed.  
We remembered the exact weight  
of the absent body  
in the bed.

If you write of raids,  
write also of milk souring,  
of the loom left warped,  
of the dog waiting at the door  
until snow made him wise.

I looked inland.

The farms were electric now,  
the roads numbered,  
the hills stitched with wire.  
But under everything  
the same dark peat  
kept its slow fire.

I asked them—  
or thought I asked—  
what I should do  
with the anger I had carried north,  
wrapped carefully,  
like a family knife.

For whom is it sharpened?  
said the drowned one.

Against whom is it honest?  
said the burned.

Will it open bread?  
said the woman.

Will it carve a keel?  
said the craftsman.

Will it make a song  
where the living may stand  
without becoming statues?

The sea advanced.  
My boots filled with cold.

I wanted an answer  
with the shape of law,  
a stone tablet,  
a commandment hammered flat.

Instead they gave me weather.

Violence, they said,  
is sometimes the door  
history leaves unbarred.  
But enter it knowing  
the room will change you.

Memory, they said,  
is a debt  
paid not by accuracy alone  
but by attention.

Craft, they said,  
is love  
that has accepted limits.

Poetry, they said,  
is the oar-stroke  
between what happened  
and what could be borne.

Then the wind shifted.

For a moment the whole coast  
seemed built of listening:  
the cliff, the sheep-path,  
the iron-colored pools,  
the town with its windows  
lit against afternoon.

I understood nothing.  
Or almost nothing.

Only this:

that the dead do not want  
our worship.  
They are tired of helmets,  
tired of flames,  
tired of being summoned  
whenever the living need permission.

They want us to make well.

A hinge.  
A cradle.  
A judgment.  
A verse.

To make well  
is not to make harmless.  
The sea is well-made  
and kills without malice.

To make well  
is to know the grain,  
to honor weight,  
to strike only  
what must be struck,  
to leave space  
for the breath after.

I took out my notebook.

The paper softened in the rain.  
The first words failed.  
The second also.

Good, said the dead.

Now begin.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a literary passage that sounds like an Irish Nobel laureate reflecting on Norse history, the Atlantic, archaeology, and the burden of inherited bloodshed, ending with counsel to a poet.
counterfactuals.output:
The sea keeps its own annals, written in salt and rubbed out by the next weather.

All along the western rocks, where the Atlantic shoulders in with its old, unappeasable strength, one hears the past not as a story but as a pressure: the keel on the shingle, the oar in the rowlock, the iron bite of a foreign tongue entering the mouth of a place. The Norse came out of their grey fjords with ravens on their sails and hunger in their houses, and they left behind more than burned beams and hoards of hacked silver. They left names in the land, a hard music in the bays, a memory of arrival that was also seizure, trade that was also terror, settlement that was also wound.

The archaeologist, kneeling in a square of opened earth, has the truest posture before history. Not triumph, not accusation only, but attention. A brooch greened by centuries, a comb of bone, a child’s bead, a sword gone soft with rust—each thing lifted from the dark asks to be handled without haste. The dead do not speak plainly. They give us fragments, and we must resist making them innocent or monstrous too quickly. Under the turf, the raider and the farmer, the monk and the slave, the boatbuilder and the buried child, are all returned to the same silence, though not to the same justice.

Blood remembers, or we say it does, because we need a figure for what will not leave us. The inherited quarrel comes down like weather, like a damp in the walls. Men are born into aftermaths and taught to call them destiny. Yet no vein is a verdict. What was done by the hand of an ancestor is not undone by denial, nor is it healed by rehearsing the grievance until it grows sacred. There must be another labor: to take the old iron out of the story, hold it up to the light, and know it for what it is—weapon, relic, warning.

And so, poet, go to the shore at low tide. Listen where the stones click and the kelp drags its dark ropes. Learn from the spade and the tide alike: uncover, but do not gloat; remember, but do not enthrone revenge. Let your words be clear enough to bear witness and deep enough to forgive nothing cheaply. Sing from the wound, if you must—but do not make a home in it.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an imitation of a dark Northern European mythic poem, full of kennings and harsh imagery, where a longship speaks to the narrator about history, trade, revenge, and writing in darkness.
counterfactuals.output:
**The Keel in the Black Fjord**

I stood where the gulls gnawed twilight,  
where the sea-wolf mouthed the stones,  
and night, that raven-cloak,  
was clasped with one cold star.

There the longship lay, land-weary,  
rib-cage tarred and frost-bitten,  
oar-holes staring like blind wounds,  
dragon-head dumb with salt.  
Its sail was furled—  
a blood-moon’s hide, wind-flayed,  
patched by dead men’s daughters.

Then spoke the keel,  
oak-bone of kings,  
wave-horse, corpse-bearer,  
treasure-hungerer:

“I remember.”

Its voice was tar in winter,  
iron dragged over slate.

“I remember the first axe  
that opened the throat of the forest.  
A man sang to me then,  
his beard full of chips,  
his hands red with resin.  
He called me swan-road stallion,  
called me bride of the storm.  
He did not call me grave—  
not yet.

“I carried amber, seal-fat,  
black furs, walrus teeth,  
and silver bitten from foreign kings.  
I knew the soft clink of scales,  
the trader’s smile, knife-thin,  
the oath-ring warmed by lying palms.  
Eastward I nosed through river-mist,  
past reed and fortress,  
past markets where slaves stood  
like winter trees stripped of names.

“Men praise trade  
as if it were honey on bread.  
But barter has teeth.  
The hand that weighs silk  
has weighed a skull.  
The tongue that speaks peace  
counts spearheads in sleep.  
Gold is a sun-fragment,  
yes—  
but it burns holes in the purse,  
then in the kin,  
then in the heart’s hall.”

The tide lifted it slightly,  
and the old ship creaked,  
a gallows remembering rope.

“I remember revenge,” it said.  
“Revenge, that red ale  
poured for the dead.  
I carried sons over corpse-cold water  
to answer fathers.  
I carried brothers with wolf-eyes,  
wives with whetstones,  
thralls who dreamed of masters’ blood.

“At dawn the shields sang.  
At noon the ravens wrote  
their black runes on the field.  
By dusk the sword-storm slept,  
and I took aboard the living,  
fewer than before,  
and the dead,  
heavier than iron.

“Do you know revenge, ink-man?  
It is a fire in a sealed house.  
It warms no one long.  
It eats beams, beds, cradles,  
the high-seat, the carved gods,  
the doorpost marked for luck.  
Last of all it eats the avenger,  
who sits in ash  
calling the ash justice.”

The fjord darkened.  
Clouds dragged their bellies  
over the mountain’s broken teeth.  
Far off, thunder muttered  
like a giant under burial stones.

I said to the ship:  
“Why speak to me,  
old wave-corpse,  
tar-black memory chest?  
My sword is a reed.  
My shield is wax.  
I make no widows.”

The longship laughed—  
a cracking of frozen oars.

“No widows?  
You carve absence.  
You bind breath to marks.  
You make men walk  
after worms have crowned them.

“The skald in the smoke-hole hall  
threw words like spears.  
You scratch them in darkness.  
He had mead, harp, fire,  
faces ringed around him.  
You have a lamp’s weak eye,  
a table, a hand cramped by winter,  
and outside, the night  
leaning like a bear on the wall.

“Still you do his work.  
You are a bone-picker.  
You are a grave-robber.  
You steal the dead from silence  
and sell them to dawn.

“Write, then.  
Write of hide-sailed hunger,  
of the whale-road whitening  
under moon’s corpse-light.  
Write of merchants kissing coins,  
of kings feeding eagles,  
of mothers who know by the footstep  
which son has not returned.

“Write of history—  
not as a hall of banners,  
but as a ditch after battle,  
rain filling mouths.  
Write of trade—  
not as bright exchange,  
but as a net where every knot  
is a bargain with need.  
Write of revenge—  
not as song-gold,  
but as rust on the family blade.  
Write of darkness—  
for all writing is darkness first,  
a coal-mine under the skull,  
where the hand digs  
until it finds a buried ember.”

The star went out.  
The fjord became a black horn  
brimming with wind.  
I heard the dead rowers then,  
not rowing,  
only waiting—  
hands on oars of shadow,  
eyes like nail-heads  
under the sea.

The ship whispered:

“Once I was forest.  
Once birds nested in me.  
Once I drank sun through leaves.  
Then men made me a road  
for greed, glory, grief.  
Now I rot beside the tide,  
and beetles read me  
better than kings did.

“But you—  
little night-carver,  
rune-worm, ash-scribe—  
take this from me:

“All voyages end in earth.  
All markets close in frost.  
All blood-prices fail.  
All names go down  
unless a dark hand  
lifts them,  
cuts them,  
blackens them  
into the skin of time.”

Then silence returned,  
wearing iron shoes.

I bent above my page.  
The ink shone like seal-blood.  
The wind pressed its blue mouth  
to the door.

And in the long cold  
before morning,  
I wrote by no light  
but the ship’s remembered burning.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a richly metaphorical prose-poetry excerpt about the North Atlantic, Viking settlements, rusted swords, stone ships, and ancestral voices warning the poet not to expect easy illumination.
counterfactuals.output:
In the North Atlantic, the light does not arrive as revelation, but as a blade dulled by weather—drawn slowly from a scabbard of cloud. It lies across the water in tarnished strips, cold as a god’s discarded mail. Islands rise there like the backs of sleeping whales, and the old Viking settlements cling to their ribs: turf-roofed, wind-gnawed, half-swallowed by moss and rumor. Hearths gone dark. Doorways narrowed into questions. The sea keeps chewing the names of the dead and spitting them back as salt.

I have walked where the longhouses were, where sheep crop the silence down to its roots, where a rusted sword was found under black soil, less weapon now than weather-vane for memory. Its iron had bloomed into red flowers of decay, a whole autumn of battle condensed in the hand. I lifted nothing; the earth had claimed its evidence. Still, I felt the hilt in my palm as one feels a pulse through a wall.

Beyond the settlement, stone ships were moored forever in the grass—keels of granite, ribs of lichen, their crews reduced to wind. They had not sailed toward Valhalla, nor home, nor history, but into that harbor where all departures become shape. Around them the gulls cried like hinges on the door of the world.

And then the ancestral voices came—not as thunder, not as runes igniting blue in the mind, but as a hoarse counsel braided into the gale:

Do not think the dark will open for you because you have asked beautifully.  
Do not expect the past to raise its lantern simply because you stand in its rain.  
Illumination is not a harbor-fire. It is the brief wet gleam on a rusted sword before night takes it back.  

So I stayed there, unschooled and salt-stung, while the North Atlantic turned its immense black pages, and the dead, with their mouths full of seaweed and starlight, warned me to love the obscurity that fathers all seeing.
